key_insight: The paper shows that pretraining data can be poisoned even in large, heterogeneous corpora—not just curated sources like Wikipedia—by exploiting computational propaganda tactics. This makes harmful model behaviors harder to spot and defend against during data collection and preprocessing.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of understanding whether poisoning attacks on pretraining data remain feasible at real-world scale, especially when data passes through curation pipelines that filter, rank, or transform sources before training.
method: Constructs poisoning attacks that target pretraining data beyond a single well-known source, aiming to survive realistic data collection and curation steps.
Evaluates how poisoned content interacts with data curation pipelines and whether it can persist into the final training corpus.
Assesses the feasibility of inducing harmful or undesirable model behaviors from poisoned pretraining data in large-scale settings.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights a supply-chain security risk in pretraining pipelines: harmful data can be introduced before training and may evade standard filters. It implies that dataset governance, source vetting, and pipeline-aware defenses are essential for safer LMs.

paper_title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
paper_authors: Victoria Graf, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, David Kohlbrenner, Kyle Lo
